Before we became parents, my husband and I said we’d probably abort for DS as well. Wowzer! We were total ableist dumb dumbs back then. My son doesn’t have DS, but he has other special needs and we’ve met adults and children in the last several years that completely have opened our minds to what a lovely and wonder life it is! It’s an adventure - yes very scary at times- but worth every single second. I just feel sad they were too scared of a “glitch” or “error” to trust they could be wonderful parents and have a wonderful child and life together.

We should have a larger conversation about how Japan has figured out how to delete the genome to cause DS. That is true eugenics. If the cost of raising a “healthy” child in the USA rn is 1.9 MILLION dollars, from birth to 18, then yes, I empathize with people who are afraid to have children with health issues. I work with kids who live with DS and they are bundles of joy, and even when some are aggressive, they are beautiful souls to be around. But the medical issues I have seen them go through, is heart breaking. They live shorter lives, the data backs that up. So I don’t think we can just boil it down to “ableism”. We live in a s county where being ill, chronically ill, or having a genetic mutation, can be a death sentence, just from my being able to afford care. My physical issues are way different than those with DS, but navigating the medical and disability system, has made me realize they make it hard on purpose, so that people di3 before having the change to get barely enough money to live on, or be sent to a facility with year long waitlists, from the government. It makes me sad, as there are many conditions that impact health, and I agree that the over arching implication is a form of ableism. And obviously we can’t plan for our children’s health, after they are born or later in life. But when we live in a society that punishes, and quite frankly k1lls its chronically ill and disabled, I feel at the end of the day, it’s MY BODY, MY CHOICE, and that applies to this situation too. I highly recommend reading literature, or “the invisible kingdom” that talk about how ableism through barriers to medical care, barriers to fresh water and Whole Foods, barriers to education, the list goes on, is ingrained in our society, and how the cogs of our capitalism machine depend on it. I wish we could have a more nuanced convo about this than just automatically saying it’s done right 100% ableism rhetoric; it’s nuanced. My heart breaks for the people with DS and families with loved members, who have to see that video however.
